growth_story.headline: Brunei's income per person sits far below its 1979 peak, as ageing oil fields have kept growth flat or falling despite a push into refining.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Brunei peaked in 1979. By 2025 it was 69.4 percent below that peak, and lower even than in 1974, the first year of the record. From 1990 to 1998 it fell by 2.1 percent a year on average, and the sources we found do not explain this era; from 1999 to 2006 it edged up by 0.7 percent a year. From 2007 to 2016 it fell by 2.5 percent a year: oil output declined as offshore fields aged, and oil and gas prices dropped after 2014. Since 2017 it has been flat, at 0.0 percent a year, as a new oil field and a large refinery and petrochemical plant lifted output at times, while recessions in 2021 and 2022 and maintenance stoppages from late 2024 into 2025 pulled it back.

threads.title: Ageing offshore oil fields
threads.text: The IMF says oil output has been falling since 2006 as the offshore fields age. The new Salman field has only partly offset the decline, and the ADB warns that outages and maintenance on ageing facilities could hold back production.

threads.title: Falling output, then falling prices
threads.text: In 2019 the IMF described an economy adjusting to falling oil production since 2010 and lower oil and gas prices since 2014. Both fall within the 2007 to 2016 era, when income per person fell by 2.5 percent a year on average.

threads.text: The long-term plan, Wawasan 2035 (Vision 2035), backs downstream oil and gas, food, tourism, ICT and services. The first phase of a large refinery and petrochemical plant helped raise the non-oil share of output, and its second phase is due to finish at the end of 2028.

threads.text: The economy shrank in 2021 and 2022 and recovered in 2023, mainly on the non-oil economy. Income per person grew by 3.2 percent in 2024, but maintenance on gas and LNG plants then pushed output down again from late 2024 into 2025.

since_last_year.text: The economy shrank from late 2024 into the second half of 2025 as gas and LNG plants went down for maintenance, and income per person slipped by 0.1 percent in 2025. In early 2026 oil and gas output kept growing, but the non-oil economy shrank in the first quarter, and in September the ADB cut its growth forecast for 2026.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes progress in diversification, with the non-oil share of output rising sharply since 2003. Over the same years income per person fell, from 38,595 in 2003 to 29,531 in 2025 (constant dollars), and it has barely moved since 2016. A larger non-oil share can come from a shrinking oil sector as well as a growing non-oil one, so the sources' story of progress and the data's story of a long decline can both be partly true.
